newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Ex-apartheid spy denies role in Palme murder.
newsitem.headline: Ex-apartheid spy denies role in Palme murder.

text.p: Former apartheid spy Craig Williamson denied on Friday charges by a South African police colleague that he was behind the 1986 killing of Swedish Prime Minister Olof Palme.

"It's crazy," Williamson told Reuters in the Angolan capital of Luanda, where he has interests in the diamond industry. "It is enough to answer for what we did, but this is absurd. It came out in a Swedish newspaper six years ago and I denied it then and I shall deny it again."
Williamson's fellow-agent Eugene de Kock, former head of an apartheid hit squad, told a court in Pretoria that the Palme murder was part of a Williamson project called "Operation Long Reach".

De Kock said he had first-hand information that Williamson was involved in killing the Swedish prime minister, a staunch supporter of Nelson Mandela's African National Congress which was a banned liberation movement at the time but now rules the country.

Williamson, speaking as he left his Luanda hotel for Angola's northern diamond mining region, said he would reject de Kock's charges when he testified before South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission shortly.
"The man either has a hidden agenda, or if he actually believes what he is saying, then he is nuts. The system has made him what he is," Williamson said.

"This is a nightmare. I am trying to get on with my life," he said, adding that reports of South African involvement in the Palme murder first emerged in the 1980s as part of a Soviet disinformation campaign.
"Somebody who started this is laughing today," Williamson said.
"Operation Long Reach was an absolutely straight intelligence operation and nothing more. We had an intelligence network throughout Africa and also in Washington," he said.
Williamson said he had known de Kock well when they were both involved in police anti-guerrilla operations in southern Angola in the 1980s.
Deputy South African Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad told reporters de Kock's accusations were serious.
"We are waiting for fuller details. It has serious implications for our foreign policy but we would like to substantiate these allegations," he said.
A member of the attorney-general's staff, Antoinette de Jager, said her office would conduct a full investigation of de Kock's allegations.
"All claims made by Mr de Kock will be thoroughly investigated, but I do not want to discuss the details of his allegations," she said.
De Kock named Williamson while testifying for a lenient sentence in his murder trial. He has been convicted of six murders and a series of other crimes.
In Stockholm, the head of the Palme murder investigation said Sweden might send detectives to South Africa to interview Williamson.

"It's hard to make any proper evaluation of this information in the first place, but the fact that de Kock is the former head of the South African security forces lends a different type of credibility to his story," Solveig Riberdahl said.
Williamson has said he intends to seek amnesty from the South African truth commission for bombings and other acts he committed against opponents of apartheid.
The commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, was set up to investigate human rights abuses by all sides during the 33 years after the ANC launched its armed struggle in 1960.
